opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's great to be here.

For many years, autonomous driving was built as a modular pipeline: perception, prediction, planning, and control, each a separate system with its own models and lots of hand-written rules. That approach got us quite far, but it hits a wall with the long tail, the rare, strange situations you can't enumerate in advance. A child chasing a ball, a construction worker waving you through a red light, a truck dropping cargo on the highway. You can't write rules for every case, and you can't collect enough labeled data for every case either.

Foundation models change that in a few important ways.

First, generalization. Large models trained on massive, diverse data learn a kind of common sense about the world. A driving system built on that can reason about a scene it has never seen, rather than just matching patterns it was trained on. That's exactly what the long tail requires.

Second, the move toward end-to-end architectures. Instead of passing hand-designed interfaces between modules, where information gets lost at each step, you can learn directly from sensor input to driving behavior. Combined with vision-language-action models, the system can perceive, understand, and decide in a more unified way, and even explain why it made a decision, which matters for safety and trust.

Third, data and simulation. Generative models and world models let us create realistic, controllable scenarios, especially dangerous corner cases that would be unsafe or impossible to collect on real roads. That dramatically speeds up training and validation.

And fourth, I think autonomous driving is one of the most important forms of what I call physical AI, intelligence that goes beyond information and into the physical world. A car is essentially a robot on wheels. The same foundation model advances powering language and vision are now flowing into how machines understand and act in the real world.

That said, I always add a caution. Driving is safety-critical. Hallucination is tolerable in a chatbot but not on the road. So we still need redundancy, rigorous verification, vehicle-road-cloud collaboration, and sensible regulation. But overall, I believe foundation models are the key that moves autonomous driving from "works in most cases" to "works safely at scale," and that's why I'm optimistic we'll see large-scale deployment of high-level autonomy within the next several years.

r001.rationale: It says generative models can create realistic, controllable corner-case scenarios that are unsafe or impossible to collect on real roads, helping speed training and validation.

r002.rationale: It says foundation models learn common sense and can reason about scenes they have never seen, addressing the long tail.

r003.rationale: It contrasts the fragmented perception, prediction, planning, and control pipeline with end-to-end learning from sensor input to driving behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the best way to answer that is to go back to how autonomous driving actually worked for the past fifteen years, because the shift is really about what foundation models replace.

The classical stack was modular. You had perception, then prediction, then planning, then control, and each module was built separately, often with its own hand-written rules and its own labeled data. That architecture got us remarkably far, but it had a ceiling. The bottleneck was always the long tail. A truck carrying a traffic light, a person in a chicken costume, a construction zone that looks like nothing in your training set. Every one of those cases needed an engineer to notice it, label it, and write logic for it. You were essentially trying to enumerate the world, and the world does not enumerate.

Foundation models change the nature of the problem in three ways.

First, generalization. A large model trained on enormous amounts of visual and language data already carries a kind of common sense about the physical world. It knows what a traffic light is even when it is on the back of a truck, because it has seen millions of trucks and millions of traffic lights in context. So instead of handling the long tail case by case, you get a system that can reason about novel situations it has never explicitly encountered. That is the single biggest change.

Second, the architecture itself collapses. We are moving from modular pipelines to end-to-end learning, where sensor inputs go in and driving decisions come out, and the model learns the intermediate representations on its own. Tesla moved this way, and now most of the serious players in China are doing the same. When you do that, the system improves with data and compute rather than with engineering hours. That is a fundamentally different scaling curve.

Third, and people underestimate this, is simulation and data generation. The hardest part of autonomous driving is not the ninety-nine percent, it is the rare dangerous scenarios you cannot safely collect in the real world. Generative world models let you synthesize those scenarios at scale, with physical consistency, and then train and validate against them. So foundation models help on both sides, as the driving brain and as the environment the brain learns in.

I would add one caution. These models are not yet reliable enough on their own for safety-critical decisions, and the cost of a wrong answer on the road is very different from a wrong answer in a chatbot. So in practice you still see a hybrid, with learned models doing most of the work and safety layers and verification wrapped around them. But the direction is clear. For the first time, autonomous driving is riding the same scaling curve as the rest of AI, and that is why I think the next few years will move faster than the last decade did.

r001.rationale: It says generative world models can synthesize rare dangerous scenarios at scale for training and validation, addressing the scarcity of real-world testing data.

r002.rationale: It says foundation models’ physical-world common sense lets systems reason about novel situations they have never explicitly encountered.

r003.rationale: It contrasts separate perception, prediction, planning, and control modules with end-to-end learning from sensor inputs to driving decisions.

astra-6.text:
I see foundation models as a catalyst because autonomous driving is fundamentally a problem of understanding the world, predicting what might happen, and deciding how to act. A vehicle has to connect all three in a very complex environment.

Traditional systems can handle many familiar situations, but the difficult part is the long tail—the unusual situations you cannot anticipate one by one. Foundation models offer a way to learn more general representations from large amounts of data. By combining visual information, language, and driving experience, they can help a system understand the context of a scene, rather than simply identify the objects in it.

They can also help us generate scenarios for simulation and testing, especially rare situations that are difficult to collect on the road. That can accelerate the development cycle.

But better understanding does not automatically mean safe driving. You still need reliable real-time control, rigorous validation, and safeguards. The opportunity is to combine the generalization of foundation models with the discipline of a safety-critical engineering system.

r001.rationale: It says foundation models can generate rare scenarios for simulation and testing, but does not clearly state that generative AI produces synthetic data to address a testing-data shortage.

r002.rationale: It discusses generalization to unusual situations, but does not identify common sense as the capability that helps systems handle scenarios they have not encountered.

r003.rationale: It describes understanding, prediction, and action, but does not identify end-to-end modeling as replacing a collection of fragmented, task-specific models.

sol-6.1.text:
I see foundation models as a catalyst because autonomous driving is fundamentally a problem of understanding the world and making decisions under uncertainty. A vehicle has to recognize what is around it, anticipate how other road users will behave, and decide what to do safely.

Foundation models offer a way to connect those capabilities. They can learn from large amounts of diverse data and bring together information from cameras, language, and other inputs. That creates the potential for better generalization, especially in unusual situations that are difficult to cover with individual rules or narrowly trained models.

They can also help us generate simulated scenarios and accelerate development. But stronger models alone do not establish safety. You still need rigorous validation, reliable real-time performance, and a system that handles uncertainty conservatively. The opportunity is to improve both the capability of the vehicle and the process we use to develop and test it.

r001.rationale: It says models can generate simulated scenarios, but does not explain that synthetic data alleviates a shortage of autonomous-driving testing data.

r002.rationale: It mentions potential generalization to unusual situations, but does not identify common sense as the reason or clearly state that it helps handle scenarios the system has never encountered.

r003.rationale: It does not identify end-to-end modeling or explain replacing fragmented, task-specific models.
